data.name: Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut
data.detailed_description:
You play Adam Jensen, an ex-SWAT specialist who's been handpicked to oversee the defensive needs of one of America's most experimental biotechnology firms. Your job is to safeguard company secrets, but when a black ops team breaks in and kills the very scientists you were hired to protect, everything you thought you knew about your job changes.

Key Features:

  • A divided near-future: discover a time of great technological advancement, but also a time of chaos and conspiracy. Mechanical augmentations of the human body have divided society between those who can afford them, and those who can’t. Opposing forces conspire from the shadow to control the destiny of mankind: a human revolution is coming.
  • A perfect mix of action and role-play: the game uniquely combines action-packed close-quarters takedowns with intense shooting, offering a vast array of character augmentations and upgrades for the many weapons at your disposal. Unlock new abilities and increase your stealth, social, hacking or combat skills: the game rewards all styles of play and approaches. Determine how you want your character to evolve, based on how you want to play the game.
  • Choices and consequences: shoot your way through the enemies, sneak up behind them without being traced, hack systems to retrieve crucial information, or use your social skills to extract information from key characters – there are always choices, multiple approaches, multiple paths and multiple tools at your disposal. Choose your playing style and face the consequences of your actions: you decide how the story unfolds in his enhanced storyline featuring the full integration of "The Missing Link" and "Tongs Mission". Find more ways to defeat the new and improved Boss Fights, use the Newgame+ feature to replay the story with your previously acquired augmentations. Learn more about the game with the developers commentaries in ENGLISH ONLY and the original "Making of"video.

reviews.review:
[h3]The Art of Not Killing Anyone[/h3]

There's a lot about Human Revolution that's dated. The graphics, the iconic late-2000s/early-2010s piss filter, the occasionally obscure storytelling and the very video-gamey presentation of a universe whose actual lore is surprisingly deep. I could spend time talking about all of that, but that's almost stating the obvious at this point. What I really want to talk about is something this game gets so fundamentally right that I'm genuinely shocked more stealth games haven't followed its example.

[b]Human Revolution understands that stealth isn't about killing everyone in the room. It's about getting past them.[/b]

That might sound like a trivial distinction, but it creates two entirely different games. One asks, "How do I get around these AI agents safely and quietly to reach my objective?" The other asks, "How do I kill everyone while vaguely caring about stealth, and what do I do if they spot me?" The latter is what so many stealth games seem to gravitate towards, even when they don't explicitly tell you to do it. You enter a room, start picking people off, and once everyone's dead, you're free to explore in peace. You might as well be playing Pac-Man, moving around the room collecting kills until you've cleared the place.

But Human Revolution does something much braver. It makes you consider whether you should engage with the enemies at all, and rewards you for leaving them alone. Even knocking someone out is a decision worth considering rather than just another thing to do before moving on.

The result is that guards actually feel like guards. They occupy space, watch entrances, control routes and force you to think about your surroundings. You have to find a way around them instead of treating them as disposable obstacles on your way to clearing a room. And that makes everything so much more tense. You're vulnerable, you have to be careful, and you can't just solve every problem by getting rid of the people causing it.

And when you pull it off, you feel like a badass for entirely different reasons. You infiltrated a heavily guarded facility, accomplished your objective, hurt nobody, and left without anyone even knowing you were there. Like a ghost.

To me, this is a much more interesting approach to stealth than treating it as an alternative way to initiate combat. Not because combat is inherently bad, but because there's something deeply satisfying about overcoming an obstacle without destroying it. The game respects the guards as actual threats that you have to move around, and that one decision changes the entire experience.

The immersive sim design helps immensely, of course. Having multiple ways to approach situations and being able to improvise when things don't go according to plan is a huge part of what makes this game so good. But it's this underlying philosophy that I find especially impressive. Human Revolution understands something about stealth that feels like it should be obvious, yet so many games still seem to miss it.

I'm not gonna do one of those cringe steam reviews that go "Music 7/10, Gameplay 8/10". As if a game -or any piece of art for that matter - is simply the sum of its parts. Sometimes one genuinely special idea or mechanic makes an experience worth having despite everything else that might be wrong with it.

Human Revolution is one of those games.

It's dated, it's occasionally clumsy, and it certainly isn't perfect. But its approach to stealth is something I'd love to see more games learn from. [b]Stealth should be about getting past people, not getting rid of them.[/b] Human Revolution understood that fifteen years ago, and that alone makes it worth playing.
